items.title: Sports Fund to be launched December 10
items.description: The Ghana Sports Fund is set to be officially launched on December 10, 2026 at the University of Professional Studies , Accra (UPSA), following a stakeholder engagement involving key players in the country’s sports sector. The launch, to be led by the leadership of the sports fund, is expected to mark a significant step towards establishing a sustainable funding mechanism for sports development in Ghana. Folllowing various stakeholder engagement, notably, sports administrations, media, and corporate Ghana, a move which was aimed at bringing together relevant stakeholders to discuss the fund, its objectives and the role of various institutions and individuals in supporting its implementation. The initiative, which began about nine years ago, is expected to provide a structured approach to mobilising resources for sports development, including support for athletes, sporting associations, infrastructure and other critical areas of the sector. Ghana’s sports sector has long faced challenges relating to inadequate funding, infrastructure deficits and limited financial support for athletes and sporting disciplines. The establishment of the Ghana Sports Fund is therefore expected to create opportunities for broader stakeholder participation and private-sector involvement in the development of sports. The official launch at UPSA will provide an opportunity for the leadership of the sports sector to outline the vision, objectives, and operational framework of the initiative. Further details about the fund, including its management structure, funding sources, and implementation strategy, are expected to be communicated as part of the launch activities. The initiative is expected to contribute to efforts to strengthen Ghana’s sports ecosystem and create a more sustainable foundation for the country’s ambitions on the continental and international sporting stage.

items.title: Djamel Ould Abbes, ancien ministre sous Bouteflika, s’éteint à 92 ans
items.description: On lui doit des formules passées à la postérité, comme celle où il affirmait avec aplomb que le niveau de vie en Algérie était supérieur à celui de la Suède. L’ancien secrétaire général du FLN, Djamel Ould Abbes , est décédé mercredi à l’âge de 92 ans, a annoncé son entourage. Assimilé de son vivant par ses contempteurs à un « bouffon », tant le personnage suscitait les moqueries chaque fois qu’il était appelé à s’exprimer en public, Djamel Ould Abbes incarne sans aucun doute l’ère Bouteflika. Une ère qu’il imaginait sans limites. « Nous serons là en 2019, en 2024, en 2029 et en 2034 », disait-il un jour, avant que le vent de l’insurrection populaire de 2019 n’emporte ses illusions et celles du régime qu’il avait servi avec un rare zèle. Djamel Ould Abbès : un parcours politique lié à Bouteflika Originaire de Tlemcen, comme le défunt président Bouteflika, ce médecin de formation , diplômé d’une université de l’ex-RDA, exerce dans la région d’Aïn Témouchent durant les années 1960 et 1970, avant de se lancer en politique sous la bannière du FLN. Député depuis 1982, il est désigné, contre l’avis de son parti, au sein du Conseil national de transition (CNT), en 1994, une instance créée dans la foulée de l’arrêt du processus électoral pour suppléer à l’absence d’un Parlement élu. À l’arrivée d’Abdelaziz Bouteflika aux commandes du pays en 1999, Djamel Ould Abbes, un homme dont il était proche et auquel il vouait une admiration sans limites, est désigné ministre de la Solidarité nationale. Commence alors son ascension : il conservera ce portefeuille pendant près d’une décennie, sous diverses appellations, avant de diriger le ministère de la Santé entre 2010 et 2012. Désigné sénateur au titre du tiers présidentiel en 2013, Djamel Ould Abbes hérite, à la surprise générale, de la direction de l’appareil du FLN en 2016, en remplacement d’Amar Saadani. À la tête de l’ex-parti unique, il s’attelle à défendre le bilan de Bouteflika, à préparer le cinquième mandat, mais aussi et surtout à entretenir le secret autour des interrogations sur l’état de santé réel du président défunt, dont l’absence de la scène publique alimentait alors les spéculations. Djamel Ould Abbes, un admirateur de Bouteflika s’en va à 92 ans Lorsqu’on lui demande, en 2018, s’il a rencontré le président, il livre cette réponse aussi amusante que dilatoire : « Là, vous entrez dans les six mètres. Il faut demander à Luka Modrić, il va vous répondre ». L’histoire ne dit pas si Djamel Ould Abbes était un fan du Real Madrid, dont le Croate était l’un des joueurs clés. Mais la formule appartient à un registre qui fera sa réputation. « Certains disent que Djamel Ould Abbes cire les pompes du président. Oui, je vais encore le faire ! Ce n’est pas une honte », déclare-t-il quelques mois plus tôt, comme pour narguer ceux qui lui reprochent son soutien à Bouteflika, à la limite de l’obséquiosité. Un exercice qu’il multipliera, en tout cas, chaque fois que l’occasion se présente. Comme lorsque la chancelière allemande, plus jeune que lui de dix ans et avec laquelle il affirme avoir étudié, rend visite à Bouteflika : « Vous avez vu la chancelière allemande tendre l’oreille au président Bouteflika et l’écouter attentivement. Nous avons un président géant, écouté par les grands de ce monde ». Malgré l’effacement du président, dont l’élocution et la mobilité étaient réduites depuis l’AVC qui l’avait frappé en 2013, Djamel Ould Abbes compare, à la même période, Bouteflika à « un lion de la savane qui terrifie les lapins et les loups quand il rugit ». Ces louanges répétées et ce soutien sans faille ne le mettront cependant pas à l’abri de la tempête populaire qui va balayer le pays en 2019. On se souvient d’ailleurs de cette image où, reconnu par la foule alors qu’il roulait à bord d’une voiture, il avait l’air désemparé et terrifié. Dans la vidéo alors relayée sur les réseaux sociaux, on voyait le responsable du FLN acquiescer aux réprimandes de la foule. La chute et la prison après la déchéance de Bouteflika Éjecté de la tête du FLN en avril 2019, Djamel Ould Abbes entame dès lors une descente aux enfers. Comme d’autres responsables avant lui, il est visé par des poursuites judiciaires. En juin de la même année, une procédure de levée de son immunité parlementaire est engagée contre lui, prélude à son placement sous mandat de dépôt à la prison d’El-Harrach. En septembre 2020, il est condamné pour dilapidation de deniers publics, conclusion de contrats contraires à la réglementation, abus de fonction et falsification de procès-verbaux publics, dans le cadre de ses anciennes fonctions au ministère de la Solidarité nationale. Une autre affaire va également l’éclabousser : celle des candidatures à la députation de 2017, dans laquelle son fils est également impliqué. Celui-ci sera arrêté au Venezuela en juin 2021, à la suite d’un mandat d’arrêt international. Visiblement éprouvé par son incarcération, Djamel Ould Abbes va connaître de nombreux problèmes de santé. Ces dernières années, il a dû être hospitalisé à plusieurs reprises à l’hôpital Mustapha. Ses avocats avaient même réclamé, en vain, une réduction de peine. Même s’il n’a pas accompli de faits d’armes à graver dans le marbre de l’Histoire, au regard de son parcours, Djamel Ould Abbes restera longtemps comme le symbole d’une période que les Algériens ne sont pas prêts d’oublier. L’article Djamel Ould Abbes, ancien ministre sous Bouteflika, s'éteint à 92 ans est apparu en premier sur TSA .

items.title: Un hombre asesina a su pareja en Parla y se entrega a la policía
items.description: María Jesús tenía 47 años y la noche de este miércoles fue asesinada en su casa, en el municipio madrileño de Parla . El agresor: su pareja, Lenin, un hombre de 45 años que después del crimen se entregó. El asesinato se investiga como violencia machista , según informan portavoces policiales y del 112 Emergencias Comunidad de Madrid . La víctima tenía un hijo de 17 años con una pareja anterior que ha sufrido un ataque de ansiedad cuando ha llegado a la casa y le han informado de lo que había sucedido. No existían denuncias previas en esa relación y ninguno de los estaba en el Sistema VioGén, el de seguimiento de las víctimas de violencia de género y sus agresores, por relaciones anteriores. Seguir leyendo

items.title: «Sutura», tisser les perspectives par les archives (2/2)
items.description: Le projet, développé par Ken Aïcha Sy, prend donc soin des mémoires, révèle des récits parfois invisibles et accompagne leur transmission par la création contemporaine. C’est en cela que l’artiste visuel béninois Eric Médéda produit une toile longue de dix mètres qui convoquent les intelligences séculaires des Afriques. Il reprend des articles sur des solutions hydrauliques dans le Dahomey, urbanistiques avec Léopold Sédar Senghor, politiques avec la Tanzanie, etc., et ce dès le début des années 1960. C’est une transmission, et surtout une leçon. « Il est important de dire à nos jeunesses qu’il n’y a rien qu’ils disent qui n’ait déjà été dit et très bien dit auparavant par nos devanciers dans l’Histoire. L’Afrique a écrit une belle partition dans le monde qui nous permet de n’avoir aucun complexe et d’enseigner tout au monde, d’enrichir l’universel », défend Eric Médéda, qui réalise dans le même temps des petits formats carrés qui font le prolongement de la grande toile. La suite d’Histoire, la transmission, le passage, c’est aussi la touche de Soumiya Jallal. Elle prolonge sa pratique et sa philosophie de tous les jours dans «Sutura». Architecte, artisane textile et urbaniste, la Marocaine explore le patrimoine depuis une trentaine d’années, pour ranimer les savoir-faire locaux qui tendent à disparaître. Sa pièce textile de couleur écrue et beige, qui ressemble curieusement à sa tignasse et son visage, répond à ce principe de revalorisation qui allie rusticité et complexité de la pratique artisanale. Soumiya Jallal a formé, à ce jour, plus de 2.000 artisans dans son pays, enjambant l’anecdotique et le nostalgique pour réaliser une pratique contemporaine qui installe le patrimoine dans l’intemporel. L’œuvre de Ko Sy, qui avoisine la pièce textile de S. Jallal, est aussi en résonance avec ces principes. L’artiste visuelle sénégalaise relie des personnages imaginaires, ou de son imaginaire, à des photos anciennes. L’esthétique de Ko Sy renvoie à l’idée des négatifs, neutralisant l’instant ou le personnage photographié, pour le verser dans l’intemporalité et l’inscrire dans « une communauté qui ne cesse de grandir ». M.O. KAMARA

items.title: CDF Munir briefed on ongoing operations during Balochistan visit: ISPR
items.description: Chief of Defence Forces (CDF) and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir was briefed on counterterrorism operations during a visit to Turbat, Balochistan, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said in a press release on Thursday. CDF Munir received a comprehensive briefing on “the prevailing security environment, operational preparedness and successful ongoing operations against externally sponsored terrorism”, ISPR said. He was also informed of progress in ongoing socioeconomic development initiatives in Balochistan. Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of the Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir attends a briefing in Turbat, Balochistan in this photo released on November 19, 2026. —Facebook/ISPR CDF Munir, in interactions with the troops, “commended their high state of operational preparedness, professionalism and unwavering resolve to defend the motherland, amidst challenging operational conditions”, ISPR said. He also laid a floral wreath at the Shuhada Monument. The army chief reaffirmed Pakistan army’s “unwavering commitment to stand shoulder to shoulder with the people of Balochistan in their continued pursuit of peace, prosperity and sustainable development”. Upon his arrival in Turbat, the CDF was received by Corps Commander Balochistan, the ISPR statement added. ISPR says 22 terrorists killed In a separate statement, ISPR said security forces had killed 22 terrorists earlier this week, on Nov 16 and 17, during multiple engagements in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The operations in South Waziristan, Bannu and Tank were conducted on Monday and Tuesday, the statement said, adding that 15 terrorists were killed during an intelligence-based operation (IBO) in South Waziristan. ISPR said the slain terrorists belonged to “India-sponsored Fitna-al-Khawarij ” — a term that the state uses for terrorists belonging to the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan. Moreover, army troops engaged terrorists in two encounters in the Bannu district, during which six terrorists were killed, according to ISPR. Another terrorist was killed in an encounter in the Tank district, the press release said. It added that weapons and ammunition had been recovered from the killed terrorists, who were “actively involved in numerous terrorist activities in the area”. “Sanitisation operations are being conducted to eliminate any other India- sponsored kharji found in the area as the relentless counterterrorism campaign under the vision ‘Azm-i-Istehkam’ (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and -supported terrorism from the country,” the statement said. President Asif Ali Zardari lauded security forces for the operations, commending their professionalism and bravery, as per a statement issued by his office. He vowed that Operation Azm-i-Istehkam will continue until foreign-sponsored terrorism is eliminated. KP and Balochistan, where security forces continue to carry out counterterrorism action, have particularly been affected by terrorism in Pakistan. On Saturday, ISPR said that four troops, including a major, were martyred while 24 terrorists were killed in IBOs in Balochistan and KP’s North Waziristan. Furthermore, last week, 74 terrorists were killed in IBOs in KP and Balochistan. The Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), an Islamabad-based independent think tank monitoring conflict and security developments, reported encouraging trends in the two provinces in its monthly report for October. Pakistan overall witnessed a significant decline in terrorism-related violence during October, with attacks falling by 37 per cent, deaths resulting from these attacks declining by 57pc, and injuries decreasing by 71pc compared to September, the report said. It added that the improvement was particularly pronounced in Balochistan and mainland KP. “Balochistan recorded a substantial reduction in militant violence, with attacks declining by 46pc, from 132 in September to 71 in October. Deaths resulting from militant attacks decreased from 136 to 44, a reduction of approximately 68pc, while injuries declined from 63 to 37, representing a decrease of 41pc,” the report said. Regarding mainland KP, it said a “significant decline” was witnessed in terrorism. PICSS recorded 40 attacks during October, compared with 58 in September, representing a reduction of 31pc. Meanwhile, deaths resulting from these attacks declined from 90 to 38, a decrease of approximately 58pc, while injuries fell from 165 to 19, representing a reduction of 88pc. The merged districts of KP recorded 30 attacks during October, compared with 34 in September, and deaths resulting from these attacks decreased from 33 to 25, while injuries increased from 11 to 13, the report said.

items.title: Nukpenu pitches sustainable welfare and data-led strategy to retain power
items.description: NDC Deputy National Organiser hopeful, Anthony Kwame Mensah Nukpenu, is proposing constituency-based poultry farms and a national digital data centre to strengthen the party’s grassroots structures and improve its electoral organisation ahead of the 2028 general elections. He believes the party must move beyond election-period mobilisation and establish sustainable systems to support its members, develop party workers and improve its performance across the country. At the campaign launch in Tema, former Greater Accra Regional Organiser Anthony Nukpenu called for greater recognition and sustained support for branch executives, volunteers, and other grassroots members whose efforts help the NDC win elections. “Their sacrifice must not disappear after the election. The party must know, support and develop people who sustain it,” he stressed. Mr Nukpenu proposed constituency-based poultry farms, each with 5,000 to 10,000 birds, to generate income from egg and chicken sales to fund party activities and grassroots welfare. He also proposed a national digital data centre to store membership records and analyse past election results, helping the party identify weaknesses and develop targeted constituency strategies. Citing his team’s work ahead of the 2024 elections in Greater Accra, Mr Nukpenu said a blueprint developed with youth, women’s, and IT teams projected 30 parliamentary seats, all of which the party won. He, however, noted that the NDC won 33 presidential seats but failed to win all the corresponding parliamentary seats. Nukpenu wants the party to review these results, identify weak areas and turnout losses, and equip constituency structures and polling agents with the resources and training needed to improve electoral outcomes. “Diagnose precisely, resource intelligently, and organise relentlessly,” he said, outlining his proposed approach across the party’s 16 regions and 276 constituencies. Beyond electoral organisation, Anthony Nukpenu proposed identifying members with professional skills and helping them access legitimate employment and business opportunities through government institutions. He also proposed expanding the party’s presence in unions and community groups, alongside acquiring a 100-acre site for a national convention centre. “We need to acquire a 100-acre site for a national convention centre, develop our regional facilities and strengthen coordination among our structures, while ensuring discipline in our security arrangements.” Dean of the regional MMDCEs and Ablekuma Central MCE, Frank Nkansah, described Anthony Nukpenu as selfless, supportive and committed to helping others resolve their challenges, highlighting his organisational experience and relationships with local government leaders, and expressing confidence in his ability to contribute to the party’s preparations for 2028. Former Ashaiman MP, Franklin Aheto, also endorsed the aspirant, describing Nukpenu as a courageous leader willing to take and defend difficult decisions. Aheto, who served as the first Greater Accra Regional Treasurer from 1992, urged delegates to support him, citing the region’s electoral significance to the NDC. Chief of Katamanso and former Kpone-Katamanso MP, Ta Tsɛ Nii Laryea Akwerteh (X), described Nukpenu as an asset deserving national office, crediting him and other grassroots organisers with helping him secure four parliamentary terms, offering Nukpenu one of his Land Cruisers after seeing him struggle with a faulty pickup. Deputy National Communications Officer, Ako Gunn, endorsed Nukpenu, citing his support for the party’s demonstrations and other organisational activities in Greater Accra as grounds for confidence in his ability to serve, while urging party members to support their leaders ahead of the 2028 elections. President of Group Ideal and former Council of State member, Dr Nii Kotei Dzani, pledged resources for the campaign, warning that “2028 is not going to be like 2024.” He stressed the need for experienced strategists to strengthen the party’s grassroots organisation. The NDC is scheduled to elect its national officers on December 19, 2026. Mr Nukpenu is among six contenders for the Deputy National Organiser position. Several constituency executives, former party leaders, and dignitaries attended the launch, and Council of Elders member Rejoice Doku also endorsed Nukpenu’s bid and urged delegates to support him.

items.title: Taiwo Obe pays tribute to late Vanguard Online Editor, Femi Ajasa
items.description: Founder of The Journalism Clinic, Taiwo Obe, has paid tribute to the late Online Editor of Vanguard Media Limited, Olufemi Ajasa, recalling their professional relationship and describing his death as a painful loss. Obe, in a tribute shared on social media, recounted how Ajasa participated in one of the first paid journalism training programmes organised at The Hub, the training facility of The Journalism Clinic, in Anifowose, Lagos. He said the training, held around 2015, had three participants from Vanguard’s Online Desk, including then Online Editor, John Abayomi, Adekunle Aliyu and Ajasa. Obe recalled that Vanguard’s Chairman, Sam Amuka-Pemu, had earlier visited the facility and promised that the newspaper would send its staff to training programmes organised there. According to him, Amuka-Pemu fulfilled the promise by ensuring that Vanguard staff participated in the training. Obe traced his relationship with Amuka-Pemu to around 1997, when his company, TaijoWonukabe Limited, moved from an office provided by late columnist Pini Jason Onyegbadue to a three-bedroom bungalow on Bassie Ogamba Street, off Adeniran Ogunsanya, Surulere, Lagos. He said the property belonged to Madam Pemu, a relation of Amuka-Pemu, who lived in a separate bungalow within the same premises. Obe recalled that when Amuka-Pemu visited Madam Pemu shortly after the company moved in, he approached the veteran journalist to introduce himself. “Money is good. See how you boys have changed this building,” Amuka-Pemu reportedly told him after their exchange of pleasantries. Obe said the encounter marked the beginning of a relationship that continued over the years. He added that when Amuka-Pemu visited The Hub shortly after its establishment around 2015, the veteran journalist promised that Vanguard would participate in the facility’s training programmes. Recalling his encounters with Ajasa after the training, Obe described the late journalist as respectful, ambitious and consistently well-dressed. “Since that training, I had encountered Femi in various places and positions. He remained as respectful as ever; always go-getting and consistently impeccably-dressed,” he wrote. Vanguard had reported that Ajasa died at the age of 44 after a brief illness. Expressing grief over his death, Obe concluded his tribute with the Yoruba expression, “Sùn re ò, Femooo,” meaning farewell and rest well. The post Taiwo Obe pays tribute to late Vanguard Online Editor, Femi Ajasa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Conservation(s) et conversations inter-temporelles (1/2)
items.description: Les Editions Vives Voix et le Fonds d’archives africain – Ababacar Samb Makharam (Faasm) s’apprêtent à leur Biennale de Dakar 2026, avec l’exposition «Sutura». Six artistes, actuellement en résidence aux quartiers des Editions Vives Voix (Point E), vont en être les affiches. Ils présenteront des œuvres qui dialoguent aussi bien avec la mémoire qu’avec l’(anti)fragilité. Samedi dernier, au siège des Editions Vives Voix du quartier Point E, la 16e édition de la Biennale de l’Art africain contemporain de Dakar et son « Off » ont révélé un bout de leurs tons et formes. Les Editions Vives Voix et le Fonds d’archives africain – Ababacar Samb Makharam, par leur présidente, Ghaël Samb Sall, ont convié la presse à découvrir la résidence et les créations en cours des six artistes qu’ils vont exposer. Les œuvres composeront l’exposition «Sutura», programmée autant pour la Biennale de Dakar 2026 (19 novembre au 19 décembre) que pour le Parcourts 2026. Ainsi allons-nous découvrir les œuvres de la Sénégalaise Ko Sy, des Béninois Eliane Aïsso, Géraud B. Cledjo et Eric Médéda, de la Marocaine Soumiya Jallal et du Congolais Olivier Fall Masey. Ce dernier, durant le tour des ateliers, a notamment intéressé les regards. Avec son nom sonnant sénégalais du Centre, il a présenté son travail devant son compatriote, Son Excellence Christophe Muzungu, ambassadeur de la République démocratique du Congo au Sénégal. La Rdc est par ailleurs le pays invité d’honneur de la 16e édition de la Biennale. L’artiste visuel pluridisciplinaire Olivier Fall Masey travaille sur une œuvre à la croisée de nos mémoires urbaines et de l’(anti)fragilité, thématique générale de la Biennale de Dakar 2026. Il a sculpté une pirogue avec des panneaux de mousse isolante en polyuréthane, et en proéminence il a réalisé des figurines et autres « traces et symboles » urbains avec la même matière polymère. En sculptant cette barque, Olivier Fall Masey évoque l’écologie et célèbre les efforts du pêcheur qui conserve ses poissons dans ces bacs. En utilisant cette matière, a priori très fragile mais demeurant un puissant isolant thermique et acoustique, l’artiste congolais explore l’(anti)fragilité. Cette notion indique de se réinventer dans les chocs et de transformer ses faiblesses en une force motrice qui marque la renaissance et la réémergence. C’est également un tableau de la ville de Dakar qu’Olivier Fall Masey montre sur des toiles A3, avec un fond neutre et des avant-plans en couleurs. Telle que la pièce présentant un car-rapide dans ses couleurs vives, tout en laissant en noir et blanc les scènes de vie et l’architecture imposante d’une mosquée et d’une église. C’est le symbole d’une urbanisation sauvage, d’une gentrification débridée et dévoyée. C’est le symbole d’une ville qui garde illusoirement des identités dépouillées de leur essence par diverses altérations, comme ce car-rapide qui est une carte postale à lui seul, mais dont les pétarades, les circuits et la fumée noire perturbent au quotidien la qualité de vie. « Mon travail pousse aussi à réfléchir sur quelles villes léguer aux générations futures », précise Olivier Fall Masey, qui porte le nom d’un ascendant tirailleur sénégalais qui avait débarqué au Congo. Tous comme Olivier Fall Masey, tous les cinq autres artistes de la résidence partent du fonds d’archives du Fonds d’archives africain pour la sauvegarde de la mémoire – Ababacar Samb Makharam (Fonds Asm) pour réaliser les œuvres de l’exposition «Sutura». L’idée est d’explorer ces images et documents d’archives en tant qu’espaces vivants de production de sens, de connaissances, ainsi que de création artistique et de connexion interdisciplinaire. «Sutura», mot et notion wolof, signifie le soin, la dignité, la préservation de ce qui est précieux. À l’heure où les débats sur le patrimoine et les restitutions traversent le monde, nous avons voulu un acte fondateur : instaurer un dialogue direct entre les territoires eux-mêmes. Quand des artistes venus de tous ces pays interrogent ensemble nos collections, ils tissent un récit commun de nos peuples et de nos géographies », explique Ghaël Samb, également co-commissaire de l’exposition avec Maïran Ma-Laügt, qui a pris la parole aux côtés d’Evelyne Diatta Accrombessi, mécène qui a accompagné la présence de deux artistes de la sélection. Mamadou Oumar KAMARA

items.title: Yalta in Shenzhen?
items.description: Shenzhen — China’s technology hub is hosting the annual gathering of the 21 members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC). But what is capturing the lion’s share of the world’s attention is something else: a planned three-way meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Russian and Chinese counterparts, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. In principle, amid ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine, and given growing Chinese influence in Asia and beyond, a summit among the leaders of three of the world’s most powerful countries to discuss these challenges should be welcome, despite or, more accurately, because of their many differences. As Winston Churchill famously remarked, “meeting jaw to jaw is better than war.” And in principle, the three leaders could usefully address what should be done to limit the proliferation of nuclear weapons, ensure that AI is more a force for good than harm, and end ongoing wars and prevent new ones. But principle is one thing; in practice, we are likely to see something else. Start with nuclear non-proliferation. China has the world’s fastest-growing nuclear arsenal and has repeatedly expressed no interest in joining US-Russian arms control arrangements until it reaches a position of parity. In any case, there are no US-Russian nuclear agreements to join anymore; all of them have expired. The three presidents can discuss what is known as horizontal proliferation, the spread of nuclear weapons to others, but the reality is that Russia and China have not reined in North Korea’s growing program. Quite the contrary: the Kremlin may now be actively helping the Kim regime to improve its arsenal as the price of North Korea’s agreement to send troops to fight alongside Russia against Ukraine. On that front, other countries have surely noted that Ukraine handed over its Soviet-era nuclear weapons three decades ago, and that the US attack on Iran most likely would not have occurred if Iran possessed nuclear weapons. The three leaders may well extoll the virtues of nonproliferation, even though they have done much to undermine its appeal. It would not be the first time hypocrisy and diplomacy went hand in hand, but that does not lower the stakes. The most that can reasonably be expected on AI is some agreement to warn one another if and when rogue agents break out of their virtual “sandboxes.” Anything more ambitious seems unrealistic given the competitive nature of their relations and how central AI promises to be to their economic and military strength. The three leaders will discuss the situation in the Middle East and call for an end to the war with Iran. But they will not do much, if anything, about it. China and Russia enjoy seeing the United States bogged down militarily in the region; they also benefit from the resulting rise in isolationist sentiment in the US. Both have contributed in various ways to Iran’s ability to fight the war. China, as a major energy importer, would prefer that the war not escalate and cause harm to the region’s oil fields, refineries, and export infrastructure, but Russia, as an energy exporter, benefits from high prices. All this takes place against the backdrop of intense Russian bombing of Ukraine and repeated demonstrations of Putin’s lack of good faith in negotiations to end the war. China, for its part, has been a consistent backer of the Russian effort, because it does not want to see Putin humiliated and possibly overthrown and sees a clear upside in the US spending its finite resources outside of the Indo-Pacific. Further limiting what can be expected from this “strongman” summit is that none of the three leaders arrives in Shenzhen with all that much strength. Trump is fresh off a decisive repudiation by American voters in this month’s midterm elections, as his Republican Party lost control of Congress and many state governments. His administration is also on the defensive for not doing more to stop the export of advanced chips by Nvidia to China. Likewise, Putin is losing rather than gaining ground in Ukraine and cannot defend his own energy infrastructure from attacks by Ukrainian drones. Xi faces a host of domestic economic problems, and his continuing purges of the military leadership suggest that his efforts to assert control at home are meeting resistance. The bigger danger might be that an embattled Trump tries to accomplish too much at this meeting. What comes to mind is the February 1945 Yalta Conference, at which US President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill, and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met to decide the fate of eastern and central European countries liberated from Nazi Germany. The understandings reached by the Big Three of 1945 proved to be little more than a fig leaf for Soviet control of Poland and its neighbors. The danger, of course, is that Trump would cede influence to Putin in Europe and to Xi in Asia in the hopes of receiving economic benefits or gaining their acceptance of US primacy in the Western Hemisphere. But that would be an abysmal trade, given the relative economic and military weighting of the three regions. A photo-op with the three leaders (even though it gives Putin more legitimacy and standing than he deserves) would be preferable to almost any imaginable agreement. Sometimes less is more. This is almost certain to be one of those times. This article was originally published on Project Syndicate and has been reproduced here with permission.

items.title: Avatime chiefs lament frequent accidents on Ho-Fume road and call for redesign
items.description: The Avatime Traditional Authorities in the Ho West District of the Volta Region have lamented the frequent accidents on the Ho-Fume Road, which traverses mountainous terrain. The Paramount Chief of Avatime, Osie Adzatekpor VII, has therefore called on the Roads Ministry and other relevant institutions to reassess the road for possible redesign to reduce accidents. He was speaking at the grand durbar of the 2027 Amu Festival over the weekend. Rolider Construction Limited built the Ho-Fume stretch as a first-class asphalt road and completed and handed it over to the government in 2016. The road, a winding mountain highway running through the Avatime Traditional Area, has several curves. However, it has recorded frequent accidents since its completion, claiming several lives. Osie Adza Tekpor III recounted how a native died on Friday in an accident on the stretch during a float as part of the Amu Festival. “Unfortunately, yesterday, we lost one of our vibrant youth on the road from Avatime Biakpa to Avatime Fume. The road that was constructed by Rolider about 20 years ago is still the number one choice by all road users”, he said. He therefore advocated reassessing the road for a possible redesign to ensure the safety of those who use it. “Those of you who travel down here, you saw the number of accidents involving vehicles on the road. That is not good enough. I am appealing to the Minister to send workers urgently to the road to assess what might be the cause of those accidents”, he called for. Osie Adza Tekpor III urged drivers to be extra vigilant on the stretch and follow the road signs along it to avoid accidents, especially for first-time users. “I want to encourage the road users to take a careful look at the road signs. You will enjoy the drive but don’t look down into the valleys”, he warned. He also outlined the area’s tourism potential, which includes Amedzofe, a human settlement at the peak of Mount Gemi, among other sites. The Ho West District Chief Executive Officer, Prosper Francis Dussey, acknowledged the request and reaffirmed the government’s plans to improve the area’s road network. He said educational projects are underway in the district to improve infrastructure while ensuring learners receive quality training. Funds raised from the 2027 Amu Festival would be channelled towards building a six-unit classroom block and teachers’ bungalows for Avatime Dzokpe Basic School.

items.title: Northern leaders have failed the people, need collective agenda — Uba Sani
items.description: By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo Kaduna State Governor, Senator Uba Sani, has challenged past and present political leaders from Northern Nigeria to acknowledge their failures and unite around a common development agenda for the region. He also cautioned politicians against exploiting ethnic and regional sentiments to seek political power ahead of the 2027 general elections without presenting concrete records of their contributions to the development of the North. Uba Sani spoke on Wednesday at a summit on Good Governance, Inclusivity and Sustainable Development organised by the Sir Ahmadu Bello Memorial Foundation. The governor said northern leaders had strayed from the development vision of the late Premier of Northern Nigeria, Sir Ahmadu Bello, who he said envisaged a united, peaceful and self-sufficient region. He called on the foundation to convene a meeting of past and present political leaders from the North to develop a common blueprint for the region’s development. He urged political leaders to engage in honest self-assessment and acknowledge their collective shortcomings. “We must look ourselves in the mirror and tell ourselves some home truths. All of us, including myself, have failed the people,” he said. The governor also warned politicians seeking electoral support on the basis of their northern identity to demonstrate what they had done for the region while occupying positions of public responsibility. According to him, appeals to regional sentiments without verifiable records of service would not address the development challenges confronting the North. However, Uba Sani commended President Bola Tinubu for supporting critical infrastructure projects in Kaduna State, saying some of his administration’s achievements were made possible by the President’s interventions. “I want to seize this opportunity to thank the President for all that he has done for Kaduna State in the last three and a half years,” he said. He recalled approaching Tinubu over the completion of the Abuja-Kaduna-Kano highway, describing it as a major economic corridor linking northern and southern Nigeria. He said the President had released billions of naira towards completing the project, which had previously been abandoned, adding that work on the highway was almost 95 per cent complete. The governor also disclosed that he and the Speaker of the House of Representatives, Tajudeen Abbas, had approached the President over the proposed Kaduna Light Rail Project. He said Tinubu had approved $865 million for the project, adding that the contract had been signed and arrangements were underway for the President to perform its groundbreaking ceremony in Kaduna within two weeks. “I am happy to say that President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, knowing the history of Kaduna, decided to approve $865 million for the Kaduna Light Rail Project. The contract has been signed. By the grace of God, in the next two weeks, he will be coming to Kaduna to do the groundbreaking,” he said. Uba Sani, who assumed office on May 29, 2023, also highlighted his administration’s achievements in pension payments, transportation, agriculture and security. He said his government inherited pension liabilities of about N24 billion but had so far paid more than N21 billion to 9,683 state and local government retirees, as well as families of deceased public servants. On transportation, he said the administration had deployed 100 buses under its free Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) bus service, recording 5.2 million passenger trips and saving commuters more than N5 billion. The governor said insecurity had previously prevented residents of some communities from accessing schools and farmlands, but the Kaduna Peace Model had helped restore access to more than 500,000 hectares of previously inaccessible farmland. He further declared that no school in the state was currently closed because of insecurity. On agriculture, Uba Sani said his administration had increased the sector’s annual budgetary allocation from N1.48 billion to more than N100 billion since assuming office. He added that more than 69,000 smallholder farmers had received improved agricultural inputs, while over 1,400 truckloads of fertiliser had been distributed to more than 500,000 farmers across the state’s 23 local government areas. According to him, the government had also facilitated access to more than 200 tractors through partnerships and enrolled over 100,000 farmers in crop insurance schemes. He disclosed that 5,000 livestock farmers had equally received equipment and production inputs. The governor said his administration was also implementing the Special Agro-Industrial Processing Zones and the Rural Access and Agricultural Marketing Project to link farmers with processors and markets, reduce post-harvest losses and improve agricultural returns. The post Northern leaders have failed the people, need collective agenda — Uba Sani appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Absa employees promote financial inclusion through Makola Market outreach
items.description: Over 100 women traders at Makola Market have benefited from a financial literacy outreach led by Absa Bank Ghana employees as part of the bank’s Colleague Volunteerism programme, a key pillar of its Force for Good commitment. Volunteers from the Compliance team organised the outreach, which engaged between 100 and 150 traders through practical discussions on savings, financial resilience, and responsible money management. The initiative aimed to strengthen financial resilience, promote financial inclusion, and raise awareness of solutions that can support traders in their day-to-day business activities. A highlight of the engagement was a session on properly handling Ghana Cedi notes, led by Judith Haizel, Director of Compliance at Absa Bank Ghana. The discussion generated strong interest among the traders, many of whom acknowledged that some common day-to-day practices can unintentionally damage currency notes and reduce their lifespan. “Financial literacy is about giving people the knowledge and confidence to make informed decisions about their money. Simple actions such as saving consistently, understanding the value of formal financial services, and properly handling currency can make a meaningful difference to long-term financial wellbeing. “We are pleased to engage directly with members of the trading community and share practical information that can support their financial resilience,” said Judith Haizel, Director of Compliance at Absa Bank Ghana. Recognising the diversity of the Makola trading community, employees conducted the engagement in Twi, Ga, Ewe and Hausa. This multilingual approach encouraged broader participation and helped traders engage comfortably in discussions relevant to their daily lives and businesses. As part of the outreach, the team also distributed aprons to traders as a gesture of appreciation and support. The outreach forms part of Absa’s Colleague Volunteerism programme, which empowers employees to apply their skills, expertise and time to create positive change in the communities where the bank operates.

items.title: Wally Ndiango Ndiaye : « Le Sénégal a le potentiel, il lui faut maintenant la méthode »
items.description: Le développement de l’aquaculture ne peut se faire au détriment des écosystèmes marins. Spécialiste du secteur, Wally Ndianco Ndiaye revient, dans cette interview, sur les conditions océanographiques, les contraintes environnementales et les exigences scientifiques qui doivent accompagner l’ambition aquacole du Sénégal. Le Sénégal affiche une ambition forte pour l’aquaculture. Quelles sont les conditions océanographiques et environnementales indispensables à un développement véritablement durable ? Il faut une eau de bonne qualité, avec une température relativement stable, une salinité adaptée à l’espèce élevée, un niveau d’oxygène suffisant et, bien sûr, l’absence de pollution. Notre littoral a un atout considérable, les remontées d’eaux froides et riches, les upwellings, au large de la Grande Côte et de la Petite Côte, ainsi que des estuaires très productifs comme le Saloum et la Casamance. Mais attention, chaque site a ses limites. Un bon site se choisit sur des mesures, pas à l’intuition. Il faut étudier les courants, la profondeur, s’assurer d’un endroit abrité contre la houle, et vérifier l’accès facile aux marchés et aux ports. C’est à ce prix que l’on évitera les mauvaises surprises. Il faut également intégrer la logistique : disponibilité de juvéniles de qualité, d’aliments, de froid, de laboratoires, de diagnostic et de moyens de transport rapides vers les marchés. Une ferme isolée, même bien située sur le plan océanographique, peut échouer faute de services. La planification doit être à la fois marine et terrestre. Justement, vous évoquez les limites. Quels sont les principaux risques environnementaux liés au développement des exploitations aquacoles en milieu marin? Le risque majeur, c’est la pression sur les écosystèmes côtiers. Si l’on implante des fermes sans étude d’impact sérieuse, on peut perturber les herbiers marins, les mangroves, qui sont des nurseries naturelles. Ensuite, il y a le risque des rejets. Il s’agit, entre autres, d’excréments, d’aliments non consommés et de résidus médicamenteux. Mal gérés, ces rejets peuvent provoquer une eutrophisation locale, c’est-à-dire une prolifération d’algues qui épuise l’oxygène et asphyxie le milieu. Il y a aussi le risque d’évasion d’espèces exotiques ou de maladies contagieuses pour les populations sauvages. Enfin, la concentration de cages peut créer des conflits d’usage avec la pêche artisanale et le tourisme. Le tout est évitable, mais cela demande une régulation stricte et une surveillance continue. Le Sénégal a le potentiel. Il lui faut maintenant la méthode. La régulation doit être proportionnée, transparente et appliquée à tous, petits et grands opérateurs. Elle suppose des inspections régulières, des seuils de rejet clairs, un suivi sanitaire des cheptels et des mécanismes de plaintes accessibles aux riverains. Sans cette crédibilité, les conflits se multiplient et la filière perd sa licence sociale. Le changement climatique et la hausse de la température de l’eau menacent-ils directement ces activités ? Oui, et c’est peut-être la menace la plus difficile à contenir. Une eau plus chaude, c’est moins d’oxygène dissout, une croissance ralentie, une sensibilité accrue aux pathogènes. Les épisodes de mortalité massive deviennent plus fréquents. Les upwellings, dont je parlais, pourraient être perturbés dans leur intensité et leur saisonnalité. Sans compter l’acidification des océans, qui affecte les coquillages et les crustacés. Les aquaculteurs devront s’adapter. Ils devront choisir des espèces plus tolérantes, décaler les cycles de production et installer des systèmes d’oxygénation. Mais l’adaptation a un coût, et tous ne pourront pas suivre. C’est pourquoi la recherche et l’accompagnement public sont essentiels. Les assureurs, les banques et les pouvoirs publics doivent comprendre ces risques pour proposer des garanties et des crédits adaptés. Sinon, seuls les acteurs les plus solides résisteront, au détriment d’une aquaculture inclusive et territorialisée. Le Sénégal dispose-t-il aujourd’hui de suffisamment de données scientifiques pour identifier les zones maritimes favorables à l’aquaculture ? Honnêtement, nous avons des bases, mais elles restent fragmentaires. Les campagnes océanographiques existent, notamment grâce à l’Institut de recherche agricole (Isra), et à la coopération internationale. On connaît mieux les upwellings et la circulation générale. Mais à l’échelle locale, pour choisir un site précis, il manque souvent des mesures fines, notamment les courants de marée, la bathymétrie détaillée, la qualité de l’eau saisonnière et la cartographie des herbiers. Sans ces données, on avance à l’aveugle. Il faut un atlas des zones propices, actualisé et accessible aux porteurs de projets. C’est un investissement modeste au regard des risques évités. Cet atlas devrait croiser les données physiques, biologiques et socio-économiques : courants, vents, bathymétrie, qualité de l’eau, présence d’herbiers, zones de pêche, accès portuaire et marché. Il devrait être mis à jour et consultable en ligne, avec des fiches par site et des recommandations de charges maximales. Comment, dès lors, concilier l’augmentation de la production aquacole avec la préservation des écosystèmes marins ? Par la planification spatiale, on ne peut pas implanter n’importe où, n’importe comment. Il faut définir des zones d’aquaculture dédiées, en évitant les zones de reproduction, les herbiers sensibles et les couloirs de migration. Ensuite, il faut imposer des normes, à savoir des densités de stockage limitées, des aliments durables et une gestion intégrée des parasites. Et surtout, associer les communautés locales. Les pêcheurs artisans doivent être partie prenante, pas les spectateurs. L’aquaculture durable, ce n’est pas opposer production et environnement, c’est les penser ensemble. Avec une gouvernance forte et des scientifiques écoutés, c’est possible. Cela suppose des comités locaux de suivi, des contrats de coexistence avec la pêche et le tourisme, et une fiscalité locale qui finance la surveillance. La méthode, c’est aussi la transparence des données et l’éducation des porteurs de projets. Propos recueillis par Pathé NIANG

items.title: ADB announces GH¢1.4m ultimate prizes for 2026 National Best Farmer and Fisher
items.description: Agricultural Development Bank PLC (ADB) has reaffirmed its longstanding commitment to Ghana’s agricultural transformation with the announcement of its headline sponsorship package for the 2026 National Farmers’ Day celebrations. This includes a combined GH¢1.4 million in ultimate prizes for the National Best Farmer and National Best Fisher. The sponsorship package underscores the Bank’s continued dedication to recognising agricultural excellence, rewarding hard work, and supporting our gallant farmers and fishers whose contributions remain critical to Ghana’s food security, economic development, and sustainable growth. The Ministry of Agriculture and the Ministry of Fisheries announced the awards on Tuesday, November 17, 2026. A high-level ADB delegation, led by the Deputy Managing Director in charge of Operations, Sylvia Naa Kwakai Nyante, formally presented the top prize packages to representatives of the Ministries. This year’s sponsorship includes ADB providing GH¢1.2 million for the 2026 National Best Farmer and GH¢200,000 for the National Best Fisher, reinforcing the Bank’s commitment to celebrating outstanding achievements across Ghana’s agricultural and fisheries sectors. Beyond the ultimate prizes, ADB will also sponsor “dinner with the legends”, previously known as the awardees’ welcome cocktail. This event will bring together nominees for the 2026 awards, past national award winners, government officials, ADB officials, captains of industry, and other stakeholders. The Bank will also hold its Farmers’ Forum, creating additional opportunities to celebrate agricultural excellence, facilitate stakeholder engagement, and promote dialogue on the future of agriculture in Ghana. Speaking at the presentation ceremony, Mrs Sylvia Naa Kwakai Nyante emphasised that ADB’s sustained sponsorship of the National Farmers’ Day celebrations reflects the Bank’s recognition of agriculture as a critical driver of national prosperity. “At ADB, we recognise that agriculture is not merely an economic activity; it is the foundation of livelihoods, food security, employment, and national development,” Mrs Nyante said. “Our farmers and fishers work tirelessly to sustain our communities and contribute to the growth of our economy. Supporting and celebrating their achievements is therefore both a responsibility and a privilege for the Bank,” she added. The DMD Operations explained that the Bank’s association with the National Farmers’ Day celebrations, dating back to its inception in 1985, demonstrates its enduring commitment to advancing Ghana’s agricultural sector. “Our commitment goes beyond the presentation of prizes. We believe in empowering farmers, strengthening agribusinesses, and supporting initiatives that make agriculture more productive, commercially viable, and attractive to the next generation. “Through our continued partnership with Government and stakeholders, we remain focused on helping to build a more resilient and prosperous agricultural economy,” Mrs Nyante stated. She added that the Bank’s participation in the celebrations aligns with its broader ambition to go beyond conventional banking and create meaningful value for customers, businesses, and communities. Mrs Nyante reiterated that recognising outstanding farmers and fishers provides an important platform to inspire innovation, boost productivity, and motivate more Ghanaians, particularly young people, to explore opportunities in agriculture and its associated value chains. Receiving the National Best Farmer prize package, the Minister for Food and Agriculture, Hon. Eric Opoku (Member of Parliament), thanked ADB for its longstanding support for the National Farmers’ Day celebrations and its continued contribution to agricultural development. “The National Farmers’ Day celebration is an important occasion to honour the dedication, resilience and enormous contributions of our farmers to national development. ADB’s consistent support demonstrates the critical role that financial institutions and private sector partners can play in recognising excellence and promoting sustainable agricultural transformation,” the Hon. MP and Minister said. The Minister noted that sustained collaboration among Government, financial institutions, and other stakeholders remains essential to addressing challenges within the agricultural sector and unlocking its full economic potential. Similarly, the Chief Director of the Ministry responsible for Fisheries and Aquaculture, Dr Afisah Zakariah, commended ADB for recognising and supporting the fisheries sector through the GH¢200,000 ultimate prize for the National Best Fisher. “The fisheries sector plays a vital role in Ghana’s food and nutrition security, employment generation, and the livelihoods of many coastal and inland communities. Recognising outstanding fishers through initiatives such as the National Farmers’ Day celebrations is an important way of acknowledging their contribution and encouraging excellence within the sector,” she said. The Chief Director further emphasised the importance of collaboration in promoting sustainable fisheries development, improving livelihoods, and strengthening the resilience of fishing communities. “We appreciate ADB’s continued commitment to recognising the contribution of our fishers. This support sends a strong message that their hard work and dedication are valued, and that the fisheries sector remains an important component of Ghana’s broader agricultural and economic development,” the Chief stated. ADB’s sponsorship of the National Farmers’ Day celebrations forms part of its longstanding relationship with Ghana’s agricultural sector and its commitment to supporting national initiatives that recognise productivity, innovation and excellence. As a universal Bank with a strong agricultural development mandate, ADB continues to position agriculture and agribusiness as important areas of its business and development focus. The 2026 National Farmers’ Day sponsorship further reinforces ADB’s brand promise of “Beyond Banking”, reflecting its commitment to empowering businesses, nurturing communities, driving prosperity and creating sustainable value for all.

items.title: China's used phones find new homes from Karachi to Algiers
items.description: In the maze of Shenzhen’s neon-lit Huaqiangbei electronics market, buyers from Africa to Bangladesh buy dozens of used phones at a time — even with cracked screens — to sell back home. “From all China, the broken mobile phones come here,” Akhtar Muhammad, 38, a Pakistani businessman, told AFP as he browsed the stacks of devices in the southern Chinese city. “We will fix them in Pakistan.” The supply is mind-boggling. As the world’s largest smartphone producer, China discards over 400 million devices annually, the China Association of Circular Economy estimates. Workers are seen cleaning and taking pictures to used smartphones at ATRenew Dongguan Automation Operations Center, which recycles and processes used smartphones in Dongguan, in southern China’s Guangdong province on November 3, 2026. —AFP As chip shortages and rising prices around the world make new devices harder to afford, the demand for pre-owned phones is also soaring. Mama, a 24-year-old Nigerian buyer, said he had bought around 40 used phones in one day in Shenzhen, which this week hosts Asia-Pacific leaders including US President Donald Trump. “They are more expensive in Africa because we don’t have big suppliers or markets like this one,” Mama told AFP . “If I buy and send them to my country, I get profit.” Nearby, another Nigerian buyer haggled with a stall owner. His haul included damaged iPhone 13 Pro and 14 Pro models bought for 1,000 to 2,000 yuan ($150 to $300) each. He plans to repair their screens locally before shipping them home for a lucrative resale. Repair not replace In particular, people in emerging markets such as South Asia and Africa, where there is less purchasing power, are turning to used models, Counterpoint Research analyst Ivan Lam told AFP. The global secondary smartphone market grew 13 per cent year-on-year in the first half of 2026 to 150 million units, according to Counterpoint. In Pakistan, people often opt to repair rather than replace broken devices, said Muhammad, who has been coming to China since 2007. “Maybe people use one mobile phone for four or five years. It’s not the same like USA, Europe. They change every year or every six months,” he said. But outside Huaqiangbei’s crowded stalls, a more formalised alternative is taking root: PaiJiTang Mall, a self-service second-hand marketplace run by Chinese recycling company ATRenew. A worker is seen checking used smartphones at ATRenew Dongguan Automation Operations Center, which recycles and processes used smartphones in Dongguan, in southern China’s Guangdong province on November 3, 2026. —AFP Inside, rows of over 20,000 used phones are on display. Buyers scan QR codes for instant inspection reports and pricing, test the units and purchase in bulk. The shop draws up to 1,000 visitors daily, with international traders making up about a third, said store manager Zhang Xiaoming. Abdul Rahim, a 20-year-old shopkeeper who flies to China up to three times a month to stock his phone and accessory store in Algeria, capitalises on a price gap of 100 to 120 euros ($110 to $132) per device. “It’s very easy for Algerians to get the visa to China. You put in your papers and in two or three days you have the visa in your passport,” he told AFP . “For Europe, there just aren’t visas… So we come here.” ‘Buy, buy, buy’ Apple devices account for 70 to 80 per cent of sales, with the rest split among Chinese brands such as Huawei, Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo, Zhang noted. Older models like the iPhone 11, 12 and 13 — losing ground to cheap Androids in China — retain strong brand power overseas, where they find a second life, explained Jeremy Ji, ATRenew’s head of corporate strategy and overseas business. A worker is seen taking pictures to a used smartphone at ATRenew Dongguan Automation Operations Center, which recycles and processes used smartphones in Dongguan, in southern China’s Guangdong province on November 3, 2026. —AFP At ATRenew’s massive processing hub in Dongguan, north of Shenzhen, roughly 30,000 second-hand gadgets arrive daily and are inspected and packed by over 300 technicians. Rising prices are also changing buying habits in China itself, with consumers opting increasingly for pre-owned models, particularly nearly new premium models, said Arthur Guo, an analyst at IDC China. Most phones discarded in China are still sold domestically, and bulk exports via official channels have not increased significantly, Lam, of Counterpoint, told AFP. For Mama, sourcing phones is still a hands-on process. “If I come, I spend a month checking (phones). I buy, buy, buy,” he said. “After I have finished, I go back to my country”.

items.title: Gov’t must improve spending efficiency, prioritise jobs in 2027 budget – ISSER
items.description: The Institute of Statistical, Social and Economic Research (ISSER) is urging government to strengthen oversight of public expenditure and prioritise investments in sectors capable of generating sustainable jobs as it implements the 2027 Budget. The institute says although the budget signals an increase in capital expenditure to address Ghana’s infrastructure deficit and unemployment challenges, government must ensure that limited public resources are channelled into projects with the greatest economic impact. Speaking at a review of the 2027 Budget Statement organised by ISSER, Head of its Economics Division, Professor Fred Dzanku, welcomed the increased allocation to capital expenditure but expressed concern about the selection and monitoring of projects. He said government must establish clear priorities for its investments and introduce stronger systems to track public spending and ensure value for money. “It’s not too clear sometimes what informs the selection of the projects. The government has limited resources. It needs to invest in certain areas. There must be a clear prioritisation of what the needs are,” he said. Professor Dzanku also cited concerns about government’s record in executing capital expenditure, noting that spending had fallen short of budgeted targets in seven of the past 14 years. He disclosed that in 2025, government spent only about 62 percent of its budgeted capital expenditure, although implementation improved to approximately 91 percent as of October 2026. He stressed that beyond increasing allocations, government must ensure that funds are used efficiently. “If one kilometre of road can cost, one dollar, and it costs two dollars, it means that you could have built twice the length of road that that money went into building. So we need more efficiency of spending,” he said. He further called for greater transparency in public procurement, arguing that citizens and institutions should be able to access information on government contracts, their values and expenditure without relying solely on investigative journalism to uncover possible irregularities. On job creation, Professor Dzanku said government must place greater emphasis on manufacturing, agriculture and agribusiness, which he believes have stronger potential to absorb the country’s growing labour force. He argued that although the services sector contributes to economic growth, it may not generate the volume of employment needed to address Ghana’s unemployment challenge. “We need to grow more manufacturing, agriculture, agribusiness. These are key if we want to create more jobs,” he stated. Professor Dzanku also wants government to establish systems to independently track jobs created under its various flagship programmes, including the number of people employed and the quality of employment provided. He said employment figures alone do not give a complete picture, stressing that wages, pension contributions and the sustainability of jobs must also be considered. On government’s reliance on the extractive sector to finance its development agenda, Professor Dzanku warned that depending on minerals and oil for about 63 percent of expected revenue exposes the economy to external market shocks. He therefore called for greater diversification to reduce the country’s vulnerability to fluctuations in global commodity prices. He also identified illicit financial flows and leakages within the economy as areas government must address to mobilise additional resources for development. “Before we think about borrowing, which is not bad if it’s efficient, let’s think about the efficiency of what we’re already spending,” he said. Professor Dzanku, however, cautioned against completely ruling out borrowing, arguing that government must strike a balance between maintaining fiscal discipline and financing critical development projects where necessary. ISSER says improving expenditure efficiency, strengthening accountability and investing in productive sectors will be critical to ensuring that the 2027 Budget delivers sustainable economic growth and employment.

items.title: Mobile money transactions hit GH¢4.9tn in first 10 months – BoG
items.description: Mobile money transactions totalled GH¢4.9 trillion between January and October 2026, according to the Bank of Ghana (BoG)’s latest Economic and Financial Data. The cumulative figure reflects the growing use of mobile money by individuals and businesses for payments, transfers and other financial transactions. Breakdown of BoG data Active mobile money accounts rose to 27.1 million in October, up from 25.3 million in the earlier comparison period cited in the data. The total number of registered mobile money agents also exceeded one million. However, registered agents should be distinguished from those actively providing services. The figures point to the continued expansion of mobile money as a channel for financial transactions across the country. What is driving the growth? Engagements with the Bank of Ghana indicate that increased adoption by individuals and businesses contributed to the growth. Businesses are using the platforms for a wider range of transactions, including salary payments. Measures by the central bank and mobile money providers to tackle fraud have also helped strengthen business confidence in the platforms, according to the engagements. Background The latest figures follow continued growth in mobile money usage in 2025. According to the Bank of Ghana’s 2025 Payment Systems Oversight Annual Report, monthly transaction values increased from GH¢333 billion in January to GH¢518 billion in December. Active customers rose by 13.6%, from 23.5 million in 2024 to 26.7 million in 2025. The report described the trend as demonstrating the “resilience and continued expansion” of Ghana’s mobile money ecosystem. The active agent network also grew following the clean-up exercise undertaken in 2024. Active e-money agents increased by 21.4%, from 404,370 in 2024 to 491,057 in 2025. The central bank attributed that recovery to improved agent legitimacy and activity following the clean-up. The report also noted that account-based and digital flows were increasingly driving mobile money transactions.

items.description: Pour faire passer la filière du stade artisanal à l’échelle industrielle, les pouvoirs publics entendent lever les blocages financiers. La clarté des procédures d’autorisation, les incitations ciblées et le respect des normes sanitaires constituent le socle de ce nouveau pacte avec les investisseurs. Longtemps cantonnée à des initiatives artisanales ou expérimentales, l’aquaculture sénégalaise ambitionne désormais de changer d’échelle. Pour réussir cette transition, l’accès aux capitaux reste déterminant. Les pouvoirs publics ont pris la mesure de ce défi et utilisent le levier réglementaire pour rassurer les banques comme les porteurs de projets. Cette démarche repose sur une relation de confiance renouvelée entre l’administration et les opérateurs économiques. « L’État, à travers les cahiers des charges prévus, rassure le secteur privé en assurant la sécurité institutionnelle et en définissant les politiques publiques visant à promouvoir le secteur à travers des avantages définis par des mesures incitatives en matière d’investissement », a fait valoir le directeur général de l’Agence nationale de l’aquaculture lors de son intervention. Outre l’attrait financier, a insisté M. Camara, il s’agit de structurer chaque maillon de la filière, de la production d’alevins et d’aliments jusqu’à la transformation et la commercialisation. L’application stricte des règles sanitaires, encadrée par le décret de novembre 2023 sur le contrôle officiel des produits, doit ouvrir aux fermes locales l’accès aux marchés les plus exigeants. « Le ministère ne ménagera aucun effort pour vous faciliter l’exercice de votre mission afin que nous puissions atteindre ensemble les objectifs assignés par le gouvernement pour le développement durable de l’aquaculture », a assuré Cheikh Ahmadou Tidiane Camara aux membres de la commission. Par Pathé NIANG

items.title: Aquaculture : Les bases d’une gouvernance renouvelée
items.description: Un an après son installation, la Commission consultative pour l’aquaculture s’est réunie, ce mardi 17 novembre 2026, pour poser les jalons d’une gouvernance renouvelée. Fort d’un arsenal juridique récemment modernisé, l’État sénégalais espère faire de la pisciculture un véritable relais de croissance face à l’essoufflement de la pêche traditionnelle. La deuxième session de la Commission consultative pour l’aquaculture (Cca) s’est ouverte, hier, mardi 17 novembre à Dakar. Organisée par l’Agence nationale de l’aquaculture (Ana), cette rencontre a lieu un an après l’installation de l’instance. Elle constitue un nouveau temps d’échange sur les orientations à donner à la filière aquacole. Les délégués de l’État et les acteurs de la filière veulent poser les jalons d’une gouvernance renouvelée, indispensable pour ériger la pisciculture en relais de croissance face à l’essoufflement de la pêche traditionnelle. Dès l’entame des travaux, le directeur général de l’Ana, Cheikh Ahmadou Tidiane Camara, représentant le ministre des Pêches et l’Économie maritime, a rappelé la portée de ces assises face aux défis de sécurité alimentaire. « L’aquaculture apparaît aujourd’hui non seulement comme un complément, mais aussi comme une alternative crédible qui peut permettre de faire face à la réduction significative des produits halieutiques », a-t-il affirmé. À l’en croire, cette volonté politique fait écho à une mutation profonde observée à l’échelle planétaire et documentée par l’Organisation des Nations unies pour l’alimentation et l’agriculture (Fao). D’après les données publiées en 2026 par l’agence onusienne, la production mondiale d’animaux aquatiques a atteint 194,5 millions de tonnes en 2024. L’élevage aquatique y occupe désormais une place prépondérante avec une contribution de 53 %, soit 177 millions de tonnes, et génère 22 millions d’emplois directs. Pour M. Camara, ces chiffres tracent une trajectoire claire pour le continent. « Avec l’innovation et des pratiques responsables, l’Afrique peut transformer son potentiel aquacole en un véritable moteur de souveraineté alimentaire et de prospérité partagée », a-t-il plaidé. Pour concrétiser cette ambition, précise M. Camara, le gouvernement a engagé depuis quatre ans une vaste refonte de son cadre normatif afin de rassurer les bailleurs et les opérateurs économiques. Ce socle repose sur la loi n° 2022-06 du 15 avril 2022 qui institue le Code de l’aquaculture et sur son décret d’application n° 2024-859 adopté le 29 mars 2024. Il est renforcé par le décret n° 2023-2160 du 6 novembre 2023 qui encadre le contrôle officiel et sanitaire des produits de la pêche et de l’aquaculture. Au centre de cette architecture institutionnelle, a précisé le directeur général de l’Ana, se trouve la Commission consultative, créée par l’article 13 du Code de l’aquaculture. Composée de vingt délégués issus des administrations publiques et des organisations professionnelles, cette instance pluridisciplinaire éclaire les décisions gouvernementales. Ses missions englobent l’examen des plans d’aménagement, les avis sur les demandes de permis d’exploitation ainsi que les questions relatives à la transformation et à la commercialisation des produits. La portée de ces réformes dépasse le simple volet administratif. La clarification de la classification des fermes aquacoles et de leurs régimes d’autorisation lève les zones d’ombre qui freinaient l’arrivée des capitaux privés. « La mise en place d’un cadre législatif et réglementaire est d’une grande portée, pouvant atteindre plusieurs niveaux, dont la garantie des financements pour le renforcement de la productivité à travers la sécurisation des investissements et l’insertion du secteur privé », a souligné Cheikh Ahmadou Tidiane Camara. Grâce à des cahiers des charges lisibles et à des mesures incitatives, les autorités promettent un environnement stable aux entrepreneurs prêts à investir dans la filière. Par Pathé NIANG

items.title: Minerals Commission, CalBank sign GH¢1bn financing partnership to empower indigenous businesses in mining sector
items.description: The Minerals Commission and CalBank have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) aimed at strengthening indigenous participation and expanding access to financing opportunities across Ghana’s mining value chain. The signing ceremony, held on 17th November 2026 at the forecourt of the Minerals Commission Head Office in Accra, marks a significant milestone in efforts to empower Ghanaian contractors, suppliers, small-scale miners and other service providers operating within the mining industry. Under the partnership, CalBank has committed GH¢1 billion in financing support to eligible Ghanaian businesses, covering working capital, contract financing, invoice discounting, equipment acquisition and other strategic business needs. Speaking at the ceremony, the Managing Director of CalBank, Mr. Carl Selasi Asem, noted that many indigenous businesses possess the technical expertise and commercial opportunities to compete for major contracts in the mining industry but continue to face financial constraints that limit their capacity to undertake larger projects. He explained that the partnership seeks to bridge these financing gaps and enable Ghanaian businesses to compete more effectively and expand their operations. Mr. Asem further indicated that the GH¢1 billion commitment represents only the beginning of the Bank’s efforts to support indigenous businesses in the sector. Welcoming the initiative, the Chief Executive Officer of the Minerals Commission, Mr. Isaac Andrews Tandoh, expressed appreciation to CalBank for taking a practical step towards addressing one of the major challenges confronting local businesses in the mining industry. He emphasised that, as the regulator of Ghana’s mining sector, the Commission is committed not only to ensuring responsible mineral resource development but also to creating an enabling environment in which Ghanaian businesses can grow, compete and benefit meaningfully from the country’s mineral wealth. Mr. Tandoh noted that improving access to finance for indigenous contractors and service providers is essential to strengthening local content, creating employment opportunities and improving livelihoods across mining communities. He welcomed the partnership as a significant step towards translating local content aspirations into tangible economic opportunities for Ghanaian enterprises, stressing that initiatives which directly improve the lives and businesses of Ghanaians are the kind of progress the mining industry must continue to champion. The partnership reinforces the Minerals Commission’s commitment to building a more inclusive, competitive and sustainable mining industry, where Ghanaian businesses are empowered to play a greater role in the country’s mineral value chain.
